title: Earn £80,000 and Lose ALL Your Child Benefit… Your Neighbours on £100,000 Keep It 😤👶 #shorts
description:
Earn £80,000 this tax year, and all your Child Benefit goes back.

Child Benefit in 2026/27 is £27.05 a week for the eldest child and £17.90 for each other child: £44.95 a week, or £2,337.40 a year for two children (over £2,300). The High Income Child Benefit Charge takes back 1% of it for every £200 of adjusted net income over £60,000, so at £80,000 the whole £2,337.40 goes back. With two kids, every £200 over £60,000 costs £23.37 (at £70,000 it's £1,168.70, half).

The twist: the charge looks at each parent's own income, not the household's. Two parents on £50,000 each (£100,000 together) are both under £60,000, so they keep every penny. If both partners are over £60,000, whoever has the higher income pays.

The bigger mistake: some parents stop claiming to avoid the charge. But claiming Child Benefit for a child under 12 gives National Insurance credits, which count towards the State Pension, for a parent who isn't working or doesn't earn enough to pay National Insurance. Opting out of the payments keeps you registered, so you keep the credits and don't pay the charge.

Sources: https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/what-youll-get · https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit-tax-charge · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-the-high-income-child-benefit-charge/information-on-changes-to-the-high-incomechild-benefit-charge · https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit-tax-charge/stop-child-benefit · https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit

One parent on £80,000 loses it all, two on £50,000 each keep it all. Fair or not? Comment 👇
📩 Send this to the parent who stopped claiming Child Benefit.

Illustration only. "Earn" = adjusted net income (income after things like pension contributions and Gift Aid). A year = 52 weeks. The neighbours each have £50,000 adjusted net income. NI credits: child under 12, parent not earning enough to pay National Insurance. Rules as at 24 October 2026; the Budget on 28 October 2026 could change them. General education, not financial advice.

facts.how: HICBC: over £80,000 adjusted net income you pay all the Child Benefit back (1% per £200 over £60,000; 100 × £200 = £20,000)
'over £2,300': (£27.05 + £17.90) × 52 = £2,337.40 a year for two children, arithmetic in scenes.py
Illustration: two parents on £50,000 adjusted net income each; neither over £60,000, so no charge (asserted in scenes.py)
HICBC threshold: adjusted net income over £60,000, tax years from 2024 to 2025; based on each partner's own income, the higher earner pays
The charge is on the individual's adjusted net income; if both are over the threshold, whoever has the higher income pays
NI credits come automatically when you claim Child Benefit for a child under 12; they count towards the State Pension; opting out of payments keeps them
£2,337.40 × 1% per £200; at £70,000: 50 steps = 50% = £1,168.70, arithmetic in scenes.py
